content.title: About
content.content: A chimichanga is a deep‑fried or baked Mexican dish consisting of a flour tortilla filled with meat, cheese, beans and spices. The dough is usually made from wheat flour, water, eggs and salt, while the filling can include beef, pork or chicken seasoned with chili, cumin and other aromatic spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chimichanga originated in the American Southwest where Mexican cuisine merged with local Indigenous cooking traditions.
Traditionally the dish was cooked in clay pots, but modern restaurants often use deep fryers.
There is a seafood version where meat is replaced by shrimp or fish.
In the United States chimichangas are commonly served with salsa, guacamole and sour cream.
The name comes from the Spanish word “chimichanga,” which, according to one theory, is a corruption of the English phrase “cheese change.”

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat filling provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef and pork are good sources of heme iron, supporting normal blood formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and spices supply vitamins B12, B6 and niacin, aiding energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of zinc
items.content: Zinc from the meat is important for immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Provides fiber (when beans are added)
items.content: Beans in the filling increase dietary fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Fried chimichangas can be high in saturated fat and calories; moderation is advised.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor pathogens; ensure internal temperature reaches at least 71 °C.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat flour tortilla contains gluten, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Spicy ingredients
items.content: Chili and other spices can irritate the stomach in individuals with gastritis or ulcers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the chimichanga hot, cut into wedges. It can be eaten with hands like a taco or with a fork and knife. Common accompaniments are salsa, guacamole, sour cream, lime wedges and fresh cilantro.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked chimichanga in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly to an internal temperature of 71 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Fig, canned – whole or sliced figs preserved in syrup or their own juice. The common fig (Ficus carica) originates from the Mediterranean and Western Asia but is now cultivated in warm regions worldwide. Canning retains the fruit’s sweet, mildly nutty flavor and soft, tender texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Figs were known in ancient Egypt and used in rituals and medicine.
Dried figs can contain up to 20 % sugar, while canned figs often have about 30 % in the syrup.
The fig is a “false fruit”; the edible part is an enlarged flower receptacle.
In ancient Greece, figs symbolized fertility and abundance.
Canned figs are frequently used in Mediterranean cuisine for desserts, salads, and sauces.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Figs provide both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestion and promoting satiety.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports heart function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols in figs protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Figs contain calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus, nutrients essential for strong bones.

items.title: Natural source of sugars
items.content: The sugars in figs are natural fruit sugars that provide a quick energy boost.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Canned figs can be sugar‑rich, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Fig allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to figs.

items.title: Preservative content
items.content: Certain cans contain preservatives (e.g., potassium sorbate); those sensitive should choose preservative‑free versions.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The syrup can be acidic and may irritate the stomach of people with gastritis.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned figs can be eaten straight from the jar, added to yogurt, oatmeal, salads, cheese plates, or used in baking and sauces. Warm them gently with cinnamon for a simple dessert.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place. After opening, keep the jar refrigerated in its original container and consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if mold appears or the smell becomes off.

pasta-whole-grain-with-tomato-based-sauc.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Tomato Sauce and Poultry, Ready‑to‑Heat

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with tomato sauce and pieces of chicken meat is a ready‑to‑heat meal that can be quickly warmed in a microwave or on the stove. It contains whole‑grain pasta, a tomato sauce free from artificial colourings, and selected chicken fillet enriched with B‑vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain pasta retains more fiber and micronutrients than regular white pasta.
The tomato sauce is made from ripe tomatoes rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
Chicken is pre‑seared without breading, preserving its natural flavor.
The dish is designed for fast preparation: only 3‑5 minutes in the microwave are needed.
Packaging is made from recyclable material and bears an “Eco‑friendly” label.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole grain pasta provides dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion and blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Chicken fillet supplies high‑quality protein essential for muscle and tissue repair.

items.title: Lycopene and vitamin C
items.content: The tomato sauce delivers lycopene and vitamin C, which boost immunity and act as antioxidants.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meal contains vitamins B1, B2, B3 and B6, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Absence of butter‑based sauce and breading makes the dish lower in calories and suitable for balanced diets.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: The pasta contains gluten, so individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should choose a gluten‑free alternative.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The tomato sauce may contain a moderate amount of salt; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Heat distribution
items.content: When microwaving, stir the meal halfway through to avoid hot spots.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the meal in a microwave (800 W) for 3‑5 minutes, stirring halfway, or warm it in a skillet with a splash of water. Serve immediately, optionally topped with fresh herbs or grated Parmesan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the package refrigerated at 0 °C to +4 °C. The shelf‑life is printed on the label; after opening, consume within 3‑4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Corn tortilla is a traditional Mexican flatbread made from whole‑grain corn flour (masa harina). Thin, flexible, and slightly sweet, it serves as the base for tacos, burritos, chips and many other dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn tortillas originated in Mesoamerica more than 3,000 years ago.
Traditional cooking uses a hot stone griddle called a "comal".
They are naturally gluten‑free, making them suitable for people with celiac disease.
In the United States, corn tortilla consumption surpassed 5 billion pieces per year in the 2020s.
Tortillas can be served soft or become crispy after frying.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Corn flour provides dietary fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Tortillas deliver slow‑releasing energy, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6 and niacin
items.content: These B‑vitamins aid protein metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with wheat tortillas, corn versions typically contain less fat.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Suitable for those with gluten intolerance.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Packaged tortillas often contain added salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: Glycemic index
items.content: Corn tortillas have a moderate glycemic index, so portion control is advised for diabetics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use tortillas as shells for tacos, burritos, quesadillas, or cut them into wedges and fry for crunchy chips. Warm them on a dry skillet, microwave, or grill before filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight bag in a cool, dry place. After opening, store in the refrigerator for up to 7‑10 days or freeze for up to 3 months.
